PCTAIRE1 is a prognostic biomarker and complementassociated immunoregulatory target in hepatocellular carcinoma

Yanling Sheng · Chaojie Zhai · Chao Li · Shanshan Zhang · Jiarong Ye · Caiwei Chen · Jinlong Yan · Xiangbao Yin

Received: 16 July 2026 / Accepted: 28 August 2026 © The Author(s) 2026

Abstract Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a highly lethal malignancy with limited effective therapeutic targets. Although the PCTAIRE kinase subfamily has been implicated in cancer biology, its clinical relevance and func­ tional significance in HCC remain poorly defined. In this study, we systematically investigated the expression pattern, prognostic value, biological functions, and immune-related role of PCTAIRE family members in HCC using multi-cohort transcriptomic, proteomic, single-cell, spatial transcriptomic, and experimental validation approaches. Among the three PCTAIRE family members, PCTAIRE1 showed the most consistent tumor-asso­ ciated upregulation across independent HCC cohorts and was strongly associated with poor survival outcomes. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses further revealed that PCTAIRE1 expression was preferentially enriched in malignant HCC cells. Clinically, high PCTAIRE1 expression correlated with advanced tumor stage, higher histologic grade, vascular invasion, elevated AFP level, and unfavorable prognosis. Functional enrich­ ment analyses linked PCTAIRE1-high tumors to cell-cycle activation, membrane-associated signaling, meta­ bolic remodeling, and immune microenvironment alterations. Moreover, PCTAIRE1 expression was associ­ ated with immune infiltration remodeling, higher predicted immune escape, and poorer immunotherapy-related outcomes. Experimental validation confirmed that PCTAIRE1 was upregulated in HCC tissues and cell lines, while PCTAIRE1 knockdown suppressed tumor cell viability and xenograft tumor growth. Mechanistically, PCTAIRE1 depletion enhanced cytotoxic immune effector activity and altered Th2/Th17 polarization, and these effects were attenuated by complement inhibition with Compstatin. Collectively, our findings identify PCTAIRE1 as a clinically relevant oncogenic factor in HCC that links tumor-intrinsic progression with comple­ ment-associated immune regulation, suggesting its potential as a prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target.

## Introduction

Liver cancer remains one of the most lethal malignancies worldwide, ranking among the leading causes of cancerrelated death1. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), the predominant histological subtype of liver cancer, usually develops in the context of chronic liver injury and is strongly associated with hepatitis virus infection, alcohol consumption, tobacco exposure, obesity, diabetes mellitus, and other metabolic disorders2,3. Despite improve­ ments in surveillance, surgical resection, locoregional therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, the clinical outcome of patients with HCC remains unsatisfactory4. A substantial proportion of patients are diagnosed at an advanced stage, and the risk of recurrence and metastasis remains high even after potentially curative treat­ ment5,6. Therefore, identifying novel molecular drivers and clinically useful biomarkers is essential for improving risk stratification and developing more effective therapeutic strategies for HCC7,8. In addition, the highly hetero­ geneous and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment of HCC contributes to tumor progression, therapeutic resistance, and the limited efficacy of immunotherapy9.

Molecular targeted therapy has reshaped the treatment landscape of several malignancies, yet its benefit in HCC remains limited by tumor heterogeneity, adaptive resistance, and the lack of highly specific actionable targets10–12. Multi-kinase inhibitors, such as sorafenib, have provided survival benefits for selected patients; how­ ever, their broad target spectrum may lead to modest efficacy and systemic toxicity5,13. These limitations have renewed interest in kinase families that regulate tumor growth, cell-cycle progression, and therapeutic response. Among them, cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) are central regulators of cell-cycle transition, transcriptional control, and cancer progression14,15. The human CDK family contains multiple members with diverse biological functions, ranging from canonical cell-cycle control to non-canonical regulation of transcription, metabolism, and cellular communication16. Although broad-spectrum CDK inhibitors were historically limited by toxicity and narrow therapeutic windows17, the clinical success of selective CDK4/6 inhibitors in breast cancer has dem­ onstrated that precise targeting of specific CDK members can achieve meaningful therapeutic benefit18,19. How­ ever, the biological and clinical significance of non-canonical CDK subfamilies in HCC remains insufficiently understood.

The PCTAIRE kinase subfamily, comprising PCTAIRE1, PCTAIRE2, and PCTAIRE3, represents a distinct branch of the CDK family. PCTAIRE1, also known as CDK16, contains a conserved PCTAIRE motif and dif­ fers from classical CDKs in its regulatory mechanisms and biological functions20,21. Previous studies suggest that PCTAIRE kinases may interact with cyclin Y-related regulatory partners and participate in non-canonical signaling pathways beyond conventional cell-cycle regulation22,23. PCTAIRE1 has been implicated in diverse biological processes, including vesicle trafficking, neuronal differentiation, spermatogenesis, and immune regu­ lation20,22. Recent evidence further suggests that PCTAIRE1 contributes to mitotic progression and resistance to antimitotic and apoptotic stress in cancer cells24. Moreover, PCTAIRE1 is located on the X chromosome and may be involved in sex-related biological differences, suggesting a potentially complex role in cancer biol­ ogy25. Nevertheless, the expression pattern, prognostic value, cellular localization, and functional relevance of the PCTAIRE subfamily in HCC have not been systematically characterized.

In this study, we performed an integrated analysis of the PCTAIRE kinase subfamily in HCC using transcrip­ tomic, proteomic, single-cell, spatial transcriptomic, and experimental validation approaches. By comparing the expression and prognostic significance of PCTAIRE1, PCTAIRE2, and PCTAIRE3 across independent cohorts, we identified PCTAIRE1 as the most consistently upregulated and clinically relevant member of this subfamily in HCC. We further investigated its association with clinicopathological features, biological pathway alterations, immune microenvironment remodeling, and immunotherapy-related outcomes. Finally, functional experiments were performed to validate the role of PCTAIRE1 in HCC progression and tumor–immune regulation. Our find­ ings reveal PCTAIRE1 as a potential prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target in HCC, linking tumor-intrinsic malignant progression with complement-associated immune regulation.

## Materials and methods

Public data acquisition and preprocessing

Transcriptomic and clinical data for HCC were obtained from the TCGA-LIHC and ICGC-LIRI-JP cohorts. The TCGA-LIHC expression dataset comprised 374 primary HCC tissues and 50 normal liver tissues, while the ICGC-LIRI-JP dataset comprised 243 HCC tissues and 202 non-tumor liver tissues. An independent GEO cohort, GSE22058, containing 96 paired HCC and adjacent non-tumor liver tissues, was used for external validation. Protein expression was evaluated using the CPTAC-HCC dataset, which included 165 primary HCC and 165 nor­ mal liver samples. Representative immunohistochemical images were obtained from the Human Protein Atlas.

Spatial transcriptomic data were obtained from the Comprehensive Repository of Spatial Transcriptomics (CROST), maintained by the National Genomics Data Center, China National Center for Bioinformation. Two HCC spatial transcriptomic samples from two individual patients were included (CROST sample IDs: VISDS000504 and VISDS000510).

The KM Plotter database was used for independent validation of the prognostic value of PCTAIRE family members. Immunotherapy-related survival analyses were performed using the GSE140901 cohort, comprising 24 HCC patients treated with anti-PD-1/PD-L1-based immune checkpoint inhibitors, and the combined GO30140/ IMbrave150 cohort, comprising 253 patients treated with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab with available pretreat­ ment transcriptomic and survival data (EGA accession: EGAS00001005503).

Detailed information on the public datasets used in this study is summarized in Supplementary Table S1.

Differential expression analysis of PCTAIRE family members

The expression levels of PCTAIRE1, PCTAIRE2, and PCTAIRE3 were compared between HCC tumor tis­ sues and normal liver tissues in the TCGA-LIHC, GSE22058, and ICGC-LIRI-JP cohorts. Both unpaired and paired tumor–normal comparisons were performed when matched samples were available. Differential expres­ sion between two groups was assessed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test for unpaired samples and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired samples. Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05.

Survival analysis and cox regression

Patients were stratified into high- and low-expression groups according to the median expression level of each PCTAIRE family member. Kaplan–Meier survival curves were generated for overall survival (OS), progressionfree interval (PFI), disease-specific survival (DSS), and relapse-free survival (RFS), depending on the available endpoint in each dataset. Differences between survival curves were assessed using the log-rank test26–28.

Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression analyses were performed to evaluate whether PCTAIRE1 expression was an independent prognostic factor in HCC. Variables included PCTAIRE1 expression and relevant clinicopathological parameters, such as age, pathologic stage, pathologic T stage, and other available clinical features. Hazard ratios (HRs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and P values were calculated.

Clinicopathological correlation, ROC analysis, and nomogram construction

Associations between PCTAIRE1 expression and clinicopathological characteristics were analyzed in the TCGA- LIHC cohort. Clinical parameters included pathologic stage, pathologic T stage, pathologic N stage, pathologic M stage, histologic grade, tumor foci, vascular invasion, AFP level, Child–Pugh grade, body mass index, survival event status, age, and gender.

Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of PCTAIRE1 in distinguishing HCC tumor tissues from normal liver tissues. Time-dependent ROC curves

Single-cell RNA-seq analysis

Single-cell transcriptomic analysis was performed using the processed LIHC_GSE166635 dataset obtained from TISCH29. The dataset originated from GEO accession GSE166635 and comprised 22,631 annotated cells from two primary HCC patients. Major-lineage annotations provided by TISCH were used to classify cells into B cells, CD8 T cells, dendritic cells, endothelial cells, epithelial cells, fibroblasts, malignant cells, mast cells, mono­ cytes/macrophages, proliferating T cells, and regulatory T cells. PCTAIRE1 expression was visualized across the annotated cell populations using UMAP/feature plots and violin plots to determine its major cellular distribution within the HCC microenvironment.

Spatial transcriptomic analysis

Spatial transcriptomic data from two HCC patients were obtained from the Comprehensive Repository of Spatial Transcriptomics (CROST; sample IDs: VISDS000504 and VISDS000510)30. One spatial tissue section from each patient was included in the analysis. Spatial expression maps were used to examine the in situ distribution of PCTAIRE1 within HCC tissues. Based on the available cell-type annotations, PCTAIRE1 expression was further compared between HCC tumor cells and hepatocytes.

Functional enrichment analysis

Genes associated with PCTAIRE1 expression were identified based on correlation analysis or differential expres­ sion analysis between the PCTAIRE1-high and PCTAIRE1-low groups. Gene Ontology enrichment analysis, including biological process, cellular component, and molecular function categories, was performed using the clusterProfiler package31. KEGG pathway enrichment analysis was performed using pathway annotations obtained from the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database32.

Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) was performed to evaluate pathway-level alterations associated with PCTAIRE1 expression33. Gene sets from the Reactome, WikiPathways, BioCarta, and KEGG collections were used32. KEGG-derived pathway information was used with permission from Kanehisa Laboratories. Pathways with an adjusted P value or false discovery rate below the predefined threshold were considered significantly enriched.

Immune infiltration and immune escape analysis

Immune-cell infiltration in the TCGA-LIHC cohort was estimated by single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) using the immune-cell marker gene sets described by Bindea et al., implemented with the GSVA R package34,35. Spearman correlation analysis was used to evaluate the associations between PCTAIRE1 expres­ sion and immune-cell enrichment scores. Immune-cell enrichment scores were also compared between the PCTAIRE1-high and PCTAIRE1-low groups.

The Tumor Immune Dysfunction and Exclusion (TIDE) algorithm was used to estimate tumor immune escape and predicted response to immune checkpoint blockade36. TIDE scores were compared between the PCTAIRE1- high and PCTAIRE1-low groups.

Immune-related signature analysis

The associations between PCTAIRE1 expression and immune-related transcriptional or complement-associated signatures were analyzed. Survival analyses were performed to determine the prognostic relevance of these immune-related signatures.

Human tissue specimens

Fresh HCC tumor tissues and matched adjacent non-tumor liver tissues were obtained from patients who under­ went surgical resection at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University. None of the patients received preoperative chemotherapy or radiotherapy before sample collection. Tissue samples were either snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen for RNA and protein extraction or fixed in formalin and embedded in paraffin for immunohisto­ chemical staining.

The collection and use of human tissue specimens were approved by the Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University ([2019] No. 053). All procedures involving human participants were performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and relevant institutional guidelines and regulations. Written informed consent was obtained from all patients before tissue collection.

Cell culture

Human HCC cell lines LM3, HepG2, Huh7, MHCC97H, and PLC, as well as the normal hepatic cell line THLE- 2, were used in this study. Cells were purchased from the Cell Bank of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (Shang­ hai, China). Cells were cultured in DMEM or the recommended culture medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 1% penicillin–streptomycin at 37 °C in a humidified incubator containing 5% CO₂. Cells were routinely tested and confirmed to be free of mycoplasma contamination using a mycoplasma detection kit.

Lentiviral transduction and PCTAIRE1 knockdown

Short hairpin RNAs targeting PCTAIRE1 and a negative control shRNA were designed and synthesized by HanHeng Biotechnology (Shanghai, China). The shRNA sequences are listed in Supplementary Table S3. Len­ tiviral particles were produced or purchased from HanHeng Biotechnology (Shanghai, China). LM3 cells were infected with lentivirus in the presence of polybrene according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Stable knock­ down cells were selected with puromycin at a concentration of 2 µg/mL for 2 days.

Knockdown efficiency was validated by quantitative real-time PCR and western blotting. The most efficient shPCTAIRE1 construct was used for subsequent functional and immune-related experiments unless otherwise indicated.

Quantitative real-time PCR

Total RNA was extracted from tissues or cultured cells using TRIzol reagent according to the manufacturer’s protocol. RNA concentration and purity were determined using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer. Complementary DNA was synthesized using a reverse transcription kit. Quantitative real-time PCR was performed using SYBR Green qPCR Master Mix on a real-time PCR system. GAPDH or β-actin was used as the internal control. Rela­ tive gene expression was calculated using the 2^-ΔΔCt method. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table S4.

Western blotting

Total protein was extracted from tissues or cells using RIPA lysis buffer supplemented with protease and phos­ phatase inhibitor cocktail. Protein concentrations were determined using a BCA protein assay kit. Equal amounts of protein were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes. Membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat milk or BSA for 1 h at room temperature and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against PCTAIRE1, GATA3, RORC, and GAPDH. After washing, membranes were incubated with HRP-conju­ gated secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized using enhanced chemilu­ minescence reagent and quantified using ImageJ software.

Immunohistochemistry

Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue sections were deparaffinized, rehydrated, and subjected to antigen retrieval using citrate buffer or EDTA buffer. Endogenous peroxidase activity was blocked with 3% hydrogen per­ oxide. Sections were blocked with normal serum or blocking buffer and incubated with primary antibody against PCTAIRE1 overnight at 4 °C. After incubation with HRP-conjugated secondary antibody, staining was devel­ oped using DAB substrate and counterstained with hematoxylin. Images were captured using a light microscope. Staining intensity and positive area were evaluated independently or quantified using image analysis software.

PBMC isolation and LM3/PBMC co-culture

Human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) derived from three independent healthy adult donors were commercially obtained from Shenzhen Zeyi Primary Cell Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Shenzhen, China). PBMCs from each donor were used in a separate co-culture experiment, and each donor was considered one independent biological replicate (n = 3 biological replicates). Each donor-derived PBMC lot was accompanied by supplier quality-control documentation, including immunophenotypic characterization and screening for relevant infec­ tious agents, mycoplasma/sterility, and endotoxin. PBMCs were cultured in RPMI-1640 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 1% penicillin–streptomycin.

For the co-culture assay, LM3 cells transfected with negative control or shPCTAIRE1 were seeded into culture plates and co-cultured with PBMCs at a tumor cell-to-PBMC ratio of 1:5. After co-culture for 48 h, cell viability, complement activation products, cytotoxic effector molecules, and T helper cell subsets were analyzed.

Cell viability assay

Cell viability was assessed using the CCK-8 assay kit. LM3 cells or LM3/PBMC co-cultures were incubated with CCK-8 reagent according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Absorbance at 450 nm was measured using a microplate reader. For experiments involving LM3/PBMC co-culture, three independent biological experiments were performed using PBMCs obtained from three different healthy donors, with each donor regarded as one biological replicate (n = 3).

ELISA

Culture supernatants from LM3/PBMC co-cultures were collected and centrifuged to remove cell debris. Con­ centrations of C3a, C5a, granzyme B, and perforin were measured using commercial ELISA kits according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The ELISA kits used included human C3a ELISA kit, human C5a ELISA kit, human granzyme B ELISA kit, and human perforin ELISA kit. Compstatin treatment

To evaluate the involvement of complement activation, LM3/PBMC co-cultures were treated with Compstatin, a complement inhibitor. Cells were divided into four groups: negative control, shPCTAIRE1, negative control plus Compstatin, and shPCTAIRE1 plus Compstatin. Compstatin was added at a final concentration of 20 µM for 24 h. After treatment, cell viability, complement activation products, cytotoxic effector molecules, and T helper cell polarization were analyzed.

Flow cytometry

For T helper cell subset analysis, PBMCs from the co-culture system were collected, washed with PBS, and stained with fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies. Cells were first stained with surface antibody against CD4. For intracellular staining, cells were fixed and permeabilized using a fixation/permeabilization kit and stained with antibodies against GATA3 and RORC/RORγt. Th2 cells were defined as CD4⁺GATA3⁺ cells, and Th17 cells were defined as CD4⁺RORC⁺ cells. Flow cytometry was performed using a flow cytometer, and data were analyzed with FlowJo software.Flow-cytometric analyses were independently performed using PBMCs from the three healthy donors, with each donor considered one biological replicate (n = 3).

Xenograft mouse model

Female BALB/c nude mice aged 4–5 weeks were purchased from Hangzhou Ziyuan Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Hangzhou, China). A total of 12 mice were used and allocated to the negative-control and shPCTAIRE1 groups, with six mice in each group (n = 6 per group). Mice were maintained under specific pathogen-free conditions with free access to food and water. Subcutaneous tumor-cell inoculation was performed by trained personnel under brief manual restraint without anesthesia, in accordance with the approved animal protocol (Ethics Approval No. RYE2024121302). LM3 cells transfected with negative control or shPCTAIRE1 were mixed with PBMCs at a ratio of 1:5 and subcutaneously injected into the flank of each mouse. Each mouse received 5 × 10⁶ cells in a total volume of 100 µL. Tumor volume was measured every 2 days using calipers and calculated using the formula: volume = length × width²/2. At the experimental endpoint, mice were euthanized by carbon dioxide inhalation in accordance with the approved animal protocol. Death was confirmed by the cessation of respiration and heartbeat before tumor collection. Tumors were then harvested, photographed, and weighed.

All animal experiments were approved by the Ethics Committee of Nanchang Leyou Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Ethics Approval No. RYE2024121302) and were performed in accordance with the approved institutional guidelines for animal care and use. The maximum tumor burden did not exceed the approved ethical limit of 1500 mm3.

Statistical analysis

All statistical analyses were performed using R software and GraphPad Prism. Data are presented as mean ± stan­ dard deviation unless otherwise stated. Differences between two groups were analyzed using Student’s t-test or Wilcoxon rank-sum test, depending on data distribution. Paired comparisons were analyzed using paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Comparisons among multiple groups were performed using one-way ANOVA fol­ lowed by appropriate post hoc tests. Correlations were assessed using Spearman correlation analysis. Survival differences were evaluated using Kaplan–Meier analysis and log-rank test. Cox proportional hazards regression was used to identify prognostic factors. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

## Results

The PCTAIRE subfamily is transcriptionally and translationally dysregulated in HCC, with PCTAIRE1 showing the most consistent tumor-associated upregulation

Given the emerging but incompletely defined role of the PCTAIRE kinase subfamily in cancer, we first investi­ gated the expression patterns of its three members—PCTAIRE1, PCTAIRE2, and PCTAIRE3—in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) using multiple independent cohorts. In the TCGA-LIHC cohort, all three PCTAIRE family members were expressed at significantly higher levels in tumor tissues than in non-tumor liver tissues. This tumor-associated upregulation was further supported by paired tumor–normal comparisons, indicating that dys­ regulation of the PCTAIRE subfamily is a recurrent transcriptional feature of HCC rather than a cohort-specific observation (Fig. 1A–F).

We next validated these findings in two independent external datasets. In the GSE22058 cohort, PCTAIRE1 and PCTAIRE2 were significantly upregulated in HCC tissues, whereas PCTAIRE3 showed a weaker and less consistent difference between tumor and normal samples (Fig. 1G–L). Similarly, analysis of the ICGC-LIRI-JP cohort confirmed robust elevation of PCTAIRE1 in HCC, while PCTAIRE2 and PCTAIRE3 exhibited datasetand comparison-dependent expression patterns (Fig. 1M–R). Among the three PCTAIRE kinases, PCTAIRE1 displayed the most reproducible and pronounced tumor-associated upregulation across TCGA-LIHC, GSE22058, and ICGC-LIRI-JP, suggesting that PCTAIRE1 may represent the most clinically relevant member of this sub­ family in HCC.

To determine whether the transcriptional dysregulation of PCTAIRE kinases was reflected at the protein level, we further analyzed proteomic and immunohistochemical evidence. CPTAC-based protein expression analy­ sis showed increased abundance of PCTAIRE family members in primary HCC tissues compared with nor­ mal liver tissues (Fig. 2A–C). Consistently, representative immunohistochemical staining demonstrated stronger PCTAIRE protein signals in HCC tumor sections than in adjacent non-tumor liver tissues (Fig. 2D–F). Together, these transcriptomic and proteomic data indicate that the PCTAIRE subfamily is aberrantly activated in HCC, with PCTAIRE1 emerging as the most stable and reproducible candidate for subsequent clinical and functional investigation.

High PCTAIRE1 expression predicts unfavorable prognosis in HCC

Having established the aberrant upregulation of the PCTAIRE kinase subfamily in HCC, we next assessed whether the expression levels of PCTAIRE1, PCTAIRE2, and PCTAIRE3 were associated with patient survival. In the TCGA-LIHC cohort, Kaplan–Meier survival analysis showed that high PCTAIRE1 expression was significantly associated with shorter overall survival (OS), progression-free interval (PFI), and disease-specific survival (DSS) in HCC patients (Fig. 3A–C, G–I, M–O, left panel). PCTAIRE2 also showed an association with unfavorable prognosis in part of the survival endpoints, whereas PCTAIRE3 displayed a weaker and less consistent prognostic

By comparison, PCTAIRE2 did not retain independent prognostic significance in the multivariate model. Collec­ tively, these findings identify PCTAIRE1 as the most robust prognostic PCTAIRE kinase in HCC and provide the rationale for focusing subsequent analyses on PCTAIRE1.

PCTAIRE1 expression is associated with aggressive clinicopathological features and improves prognostic prediction in HCC

After confirming the prognostic value of PCTAIRE1, we further examined its association with clinicopathologi­ cal characteristics in the TCGA-LIHC cohort. PCTAIRE1 expression was significantly increased in patients with advanced pathologic stage and higher pathologic T stage, suggesting that PCTAIRE1 upregulation is closely associated with tumor progression in HCC (Fig. 4A,B). Consistently, higher PCTAIRE1 expression was observed in patients with higher histologic grade, vascular invasion, elevated AFP level, and multiple tumor foci (Fig. 4E– H). In contrast, PCTAIRE1 expression showed no significant association with pathologic N stage, pathologic M stage, Child–Pugh grade, or age, probably due to the limited number of patients in some clinical subgroups (Fig. 4C, D, I, N). Notably, PCTAIRE1 expression was also significantly higher in female patients than in male patients, suggesting a potential sex-related difference in PCTAIRE1 dysregulation in HCC (Fig. 4O).

We next evaluated the diagnostic and prognostic value of PCTAIRE1 in the TCGA-LIHC cohort. ROC curve analysis showed that PCTAIRE1 had strong ability to distinguish HCC tumor tissues from normal liver tissues, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.960 (Fig. 4P). Time-dependent ROC analysis further indicated that PCTAIRE1 expression had predictive value for 1-, 3-, and 5-year overall survival (Fig. 4Q). To facilitate indi­ vidualized prognostic prediction, we constructed a nomogram integrating PCTAIRE1 expression with clinico­ pathological variables, including pathologic T stage, pathologic stage, and AFP level. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses reveal tumor-cell-enriched PCTAIRE1 expression in HCC

To further determine the cellular source of PCTAIRE1 expression in HCC, we analyzed single-cell transcriptomic data from HCC tissues. Unsupervised clustering identified multiple major cell populations within the tumor microenvironment, including malignant cells, hepatocytes, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, myeloid cells, T cell subsets, B cells, and other immune cell populations (Fig. 5A,B). Feature plot and violin plot analyses showed that PCTAIRE1 expression was predominantly enriched in malignant tumor cells, whereas most non-malignant stro­ mal and immune cell populations exhibited relatively low expression levels (Fig. 5C,D). These findings indicate that the elevated PCTAIRE1 expression observed in bulk tumor tissues is mainly derived from malignant HCC cells rather than broadly distributed across the tumor microenvironment.

We next used spatial transcriptomic analysis to examine the in situ distribution of PCTAIRE1 within HCC tissue architecture. In representative tumor sections, PCTAIRE1 expression was spatially enriched in tumordominant regions (Fig. 5E,F,H,I). Quantitative comparison further confirmed that PCTAIRE1 expression was significantly higher in HCC tumor cells than in hepatocytes (Fig. 5G,J). PCTAIRE1 is associated with immune infiltration remodeling and poor immunotherapy-related outcomes in HCC

Given the enrichment of immune-related pathways in PCTAIRE1-associated transcriptomic profiles, we next investigated the relationship between PCTAIRE1 expression and the immune microenvironment in HCC. Immune infiltration analysis revealed that PCTAIRE1 expression was positively correlated with several immune cell pop­ ulations, particularly Th2 cells, NK CD56bright cells, T helper cells, TFH cells, and macrophages, whereas it was negatively correlated with Th17 cells, neutrophils, cytotoxic cells, dendritic cells, regulatory T cells, and CD8 T cells (Fig. 7A). This immune infiltration pattern suggests that PCTAIRE1-high tumors may be characterized by an altered immune balance rather than simple immune activation or suppression. We further evaluated the potential relationship between PCTAIRE1 and immune escape using the TIDE algorithm. PCTAIRE1-high tumors exhib­ ited significantly higher TIDE scores than PCTAIRE1-low tumors, suggesting a stronger potential for immune evasion and a lower predicted response to immune checkpoint blockade (Fig. 7G).

PCTAIRE1 knockdown enhances immune effector activity and suppresses tumor growth in HCC models

Based on the immune-related associations identified above, we next investigated whether PCTAIRE1 depletion could alter tumor–immune interactions in vitro. LM3 cells transfected with negative control or shPCTAIRE1 were co-cultured with peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), followed by assessment of tumor cell viabil­ ity, complement-associated factors, cytotoxic effector molecules, and T helper cell polarization (Fig. 9A). In this co-culture system, PCTAIRE1 knockdown significantly reduced LM3 cell viability, indicating that depletion of PCTAIRE1 impaired tumor cell survival under immune-interactive conditions (Fig. 9B).

We then examined immune-related secreted factors in the co-culture supernatant. PCTAIRE1 knockdown significantly increased the levels of the complement activation products C3a and C5a (Fig. 9C, D). In paral­ lel, the cytotoxic effector molecules granzyme B and perforin were also markedly increased after PCTAIRE1 knockdown (Fig. 9E,F), suggesting enhanced immune effector activity in the co-culture system. Flow cytometry further showed that PCTAIRE1 depletion decreased the proportion of Th2 cells while increasing the proportion of Th17 cells among CD4-positive T cells (Fig. 9G,H). Consistently, western blot analysis showed reduced GATA3 expression and increased RORC expression after PCTAIRE1 knockdown (Fig. 9I), supporting a shift in T helper cell-related transcriptional programs.

To further validate the tumor-promoting role of PCTAIRE1 in vivo, we established a xenograft model using LM3 cells with or without PCTAIRE1 knockdown in the presence of PBMCs (Fig. 9J). Tumors derived from shPCTAIRE1 cells exhibited significantly reduced tumor volume and tumor weight compared with those derived from control cells (Fig. 9K,L). Together, these results demonstrate that PCTAIRE1 depletion suppresses HCC tumor growth and is accompanied by enhanced cytotoxic immune activity and altered T helper cell polarization, supporting a functional link between PCTAIRE1 and tumor immune regulation.

Complement inhibition attenuates the immune-regulatory effects induced by PCTAIRE1 knockdown

To further determine whether complement activation contributed to the immune-regulatory effects induced by PCTAIRE1 depletion, we treated the LM3/PBMC co-culture system with Compstatin, a complement inhibitor. In the absence of Compstatin, PCTAIRE1 knockdown markedly reduced LM3 cell viability, consistent with the tumor-suppressive effect observed above. However, this inhibitory effect was largely attenuated after Compstatin treatment, as no significant difference in cell viability was observed between the control and shPCTAIRE1 groups under complement-inhibited conditions (Fig. 10A). Western blot analysis further confirmed efficient PCTAIRE1 knockdown and showed corresponding changes in the T helper cell-related transcription factors GATA3 and RORC, supporting the involvement of PCTAIRE1 in regulating immune-associated transcriptional programs (Fig. 10B).

Consistent with the results in Fig. 9, PCTAIRE1 knockdown significantly increased the release of the com­ plement activation products C3a and C5a in the co-culture system. Notably, Compstatin treatment abolished these differences, indicating effective suppression of complement-associated activation (Fig. 10C,D). Similarly, PCTAIRE1 knockdown increased the secretion of the cytotoxic effector molecules granzyme B and perforin, whereas these increases were no longer significant after Compstatin treatment (Fig. 10E,F). These data suggest that complement activity is required, at least in part, for the enhanced cytotoxic immune response observed after PCTAIRE1 depletion.

## Discussion

Although cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) have long been studied as central regulators of cell-cycle progres­ sion, the biological and clinical significance of non-canonical CDK subfamilies—particularly the PCTAIRE kinases—in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains poorly defined14,20. In this study, we identified PCTAIRE1 (CDK16) as the most consistently upregulated and prognostically adverse member of the PCTAIRE subfam­ ily across multiple independent HCC cohorts. PCTAIRE1 was preferentially enriched in malignant HCC cells and independently predicted poor overall survival. Functionally, PCTAIRE1 knockdown suppressed tumor cell viability and xenograft growth, and reprogrammed the immune microenvironment by enhancing complement activation, cytotoxic effector molecule release, and Th17 polarization—effects that were attenuated by comple­ ment inhibition with Compstatin. These findings suggest that PCTAIRE1 acts as a tumor-promoting kinase that integrates cell-cycle control with complement-associated immune evasion in HCC.

The PCTAIRE kinase subfamily—comprising CDK16 (PCTAIRE1), CDK17 (PCTAIRE2), and CDK18 (PCTAIRE3)—is distinguished from classical CDKs by its conserved PCTAIRE motif and distinct regulatory partners, including cyclin Y and cyclin Y-like proteins20,37,38. Among them, CDK16 has been implicated in ves­ icle trafficking, neurite outgrowth, spermatogenesis, and, more recently, in cancer biology through regulation of actin dynamics and non-canonical signaling pathways20,39–41. Our data extend these observations by demon­ strating that CDK16/PCTAIRE1 is aberrantly activated in HCC at both the transcript and protein levels and cor­ relates with aggressive clinicopathological features, including advanced stage, vascular invasion, and elevated AFP. The preferential expression of PCTAIRE1 in malignant hepatocytes rather than stromal compartments sup­ ports a tumor-cell-intrinsic role and suggests a potentially favorable therapeutic window compared with broadly expressed cell-cycle CDKs.

Enrichment analyses linked PCTAIRE1-high tumors to mitotic regulation, DNA replication, and CDKrelated signaling, consistent with the established pro-proliferative functions of CDK family members. However, PCTAIRE1-high HCC also showed alterations in membrane signaling, ion channel activity, and metabolic path­ ways, implying that PCTAIRE1 may contribute to a broader tumor phenotype beyond canonical cell-cycle con­ trol. Importantly, PCTAIRE1 expression was associated with immune infiltration remodeling and elevated TIDE scores, indicating a potential link between PCTAIRE1 and immune escape rather than simple immune exclusion. These data are in line with emerging evidence that non-canonical CDKs can modulate tumor–immune interac­ tions independently of their roles in proliferation.

A key finding of this study is the identification of a complement-associated immune regulatory axis governed by PCTAIRE1. PCTAIRE1 knockdown increased complement activation products (C3a, C5a) and cytotoxic mol­ ecules (granzyme B, perforin), accompanied by a shift from Th2 toward Th17 polarization among CD4⁺ T cells. Notably, pharmacological inhibition of complement activation with Compstatin abolished these immune-related changes, indicating that the immunomodulatory effects of PCTAIRE1 depletion are at least partially dependent on complement signaling. Although the complement system is classically viewed as a mediator of anti-tumor innate immunity, accumulating evidence suggests that chronic or dysregulated complement activation within the tumor microenvironment can promote immune suppression, angiogenesis, and therapeutic resistance42–45. Our results position PCTAIRE1 as a putative regulator of this balance, whereby sustained PCTAIRE1 expression may restrain local complement activity to maintain an immune-evasive state. The precise molecular mechanism— whether PCTAIRE1 directly phosphorylates complement pathway components or indirectly modulates secretory factors influencing complement homeostasis—warrants further investigation.

From a translational perspective, PCTAIRE1 may serve both as a prognostic biomarker for aggressive HCC and as a stratification tool to identify patients less likely to benefit from immune checkpoint blockade alone. Moreover, the dual effect of PCTAIRE1 knockdown—suppressing tumor cell proliferation while potentiating cytotoxic immunity—suggests that targeted inhibition of PCTAIRE1, potentially in combination with immune

Second, the mechanis­ tic link between PCTAIRE1 kinase activity and complement-mediated immune regulation remains to be fully elucidated. Future studies employing immunocompetent HCC models, patient-derived organoids, and selective PCTAIRE1 inhibitors will be essential to validate the therapeutic potential of targeting this axis.

In summary, we identify PCTAIRE1/CDK16 as a clinically relevant oncogenic kinase in HCC that couples tumor-intrinsic malignant progression with complement-associated immune regulation. These findings provide a rationale for further exploration of PCTAIRE1 as a prognostic biomarker and a potential therapeutic target in hepatocellular carcinoma.

## Conclusion

In conclusion, this study identifies PCTAIRE1 as the most clinically relevant member of the PCTAIRE kinase subfamily in HCC. PCTAIRE1 was consistently upregulated in HCC tissues, preferentially enriched in malignant tumor cells, and strongly associated with aggressive clinicopathological features and poor prognosis. Functional analyses further linked PCTAIRE1 to cell-cycle activation, immune microenvironment remodeling, and unfavor­ able immunotherapy-related outcomes. Experimentally, PCTAIRE1 knockdown suppressed HCC tumor growth and enhanced cytotoxic immune activity, partly through complement-associated regulation of Th2/Th17 polar­ ization. These findings suggest that PCTAIRE1 may serve as a promising prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target for HCC.
